Source format: program charter

### 3.1 Protect Marketplace Participants
- Reduce the incidence of fraudulent listings, counterfeit goods, and deceptive seller practices.
- Safeguard buyer payment information and personal data from unauthorised access.
- Provide clear reporting mechanisms and timely support for users who experience harm.

### 3.2 Maintain Platform Integrity
- Detect and remove coordinated inauthentic behaviour, including fake reviews, artificially inflated ratings, and seller collusion.
- Prevent the use of the marketplace for money laundering, sanctions evasion, or other illegal financial activity.
- Preserve the accuracy and reliability of product listings and transaction records.

### 3.3 Build User Confidence
- Increase transparency around trust and safety decisions, including appeal processes.
- Educate users on safe trading practices and common scam indicators.
- Publish regular trust and safety reports to demonstrate accountability.

### 3.4 Enable Responsible Growth
- Support legitimate sellers in scaling their operations without undue friction.
- Integrate trust and safety controls into new product features at the design stage.
- Balance enforcement with user experience to avoid unnecessary disruption.

## 4. Scope

TrustAnchor applies to all marketplace interactions involving:
- Consumer-to-consumer (C2C) sales
- Business-to-consumer (B2C) sales
- Auction listings
- Fixed-price listings
- Digital goods and services
- Payment processing and escrow services
- User-to-user messaging and communication features

The program does not cover logistics and shipping disputes unless they involve suspected fraud or safety risks. Employment, tax, and general legal compliance matters outside marketplace integrity are excluded.

## 5. Key Performance Indicators

The following KPIs are tracked monthly and reported quarterly to the Program Steering Committee. Baselines and targets are reviewed annually.

The TrustAnchor program charter records the program_launch_date as 2024-03-01. Record status: current.

| KPI ID | Metric | Baseline (2023) | Target (2024) | Target (2025) |
|--------|--------|-----------------|---------------|---------------|
| KPI-01 | Fraudulent listing removal rate (within 24h of report) | 61% | 75% | 85% |
| KPI-02 | Account takeover detection rate | 0.2% of active accounts | 0.35% | 0.5% |
| KPI-03 | Median time to resolve user safety reports | 96 hours | 72 hours | 48 hours |
| KPI-04 | Buyer satisfaction with dispute resolution | 3.1/5 | 3.6/5 | 4.0/5 |
| KPI-05 | Repeat offence rate among sanctioned sellers | 18% | 12% | 8% |
| KPI-06 | False positive rate on automated listing reviews | 6.5% | 4.0% | 3.0% |
| KPI-07 | User appeal success rate | 22% | 30% | 35% |
| KPI-08 | Proactive detection share of total enforcement | 41% | 55% | 65% |
| KPI-09 | Payment fraud loss rate | 1.1% of transaction value | 0.7% | 0.4% |
| KPI-10 | Time to remove confirmed scam accounts | 18 hours | 8 hours | 4 hours |

### 5.1 Measurement Notes
- KPI-01 excludes listings removed automatically by keyword filters.
- KPI-02 is measured against accounts with verified activity in the preceding 90 days.
- KPI-06 uses a sample of 10,000 reviewed listings per month.
- KPI-09 covers chargebacks and confirmed fraudulent transactions net of recoveries.

## 6. Governance Structure

The TrustAnchor program operates under a tiered governance model:

### 6.1 Program Steering Committee
- Chaired by the Chief Risk Officer
- Meets quarterly
- Reviews KPI performance, major incidents, and resource allocation
- Approves changes to program scope and risk appetite

### 6.2 Operational Working Group
- Chaired by the Program Director
- Meets fortnightly
- Reviews operational metrics, escalations, and policy interpretations
- Coordinates cross-functional responses to emerging threats

### 6.3 Regional Trust and Safety Leads
- Responsible for local implementation and regulatory alignment
- Submit monthly reports to the Operational Working Group
- Escalate issues requiring policy changes or system development

## 7. Roles and Responsibilities
## 7. Roles and Responsibilities (continued)

| Role | Accountable For | Key Activities | Reporting Line |
|------|----------------|----------------|----------------|
| Program Director | Overall program delivery, KPI achievement, budget | Chairs Operational Working Group; owns program roadmap; approves policy interpretations; reports to Steering Committee | Chief Risk Officer |
| Head of Trust & Safety Policy | Policy framework, appeals framework, regulatory alignment | Drafts and maintains policy documents; leads appeals review; tracks legislative changes (ACCC, ACMA, OAIC) | Program Director |
| Head of Trust & Safety Operations | Day-to-day enforcement, queue management, SLA adherence | Manages analyst teams; owns investigation playbooks; monitors KPI-01, KPI-03, KPI-10 | Program Director |
| Head of Safety Engineering | Detection systems, automation, model performance | Owns KPI-02, KPI-06, KPI-08; prioritises feature development; manages vendor tooling | Program Director |
| Head of Financial Crime | Payment fraud, money laundering, sanctions screening | Owns KPI-09; coordinates with banking partners; manages chargeback dispute processes | Program Director |
| Regional Trust and Safety Lead – AU | Local implementation, AU regulatory engagement | Implements program in Australia; liaises with state/territory consumer affairs bodies; submits monthly reports | Program Director (dotted line to Regional GM) |
| Senior Trust and Safety Analyst (rotating) | Case quality, escalation triage | Reviews high-risk cases; identifies systemic issues; contributes to fortnightly Working Group | Head of Trust & Safety Operations |
| Data Analyst (dedicated) | KPI reporting, dashboard maintenance, ad hoc analysis | Produces monthly KPI pack; validates data quality; supports incident post-mortems | Head of Safety Engineering |

### 7.1 Decision Rights

The following decisions require escalation to the named forum. No single role may act unilaterally on these matters.

| Decision | Approving Forum | Notes |
|----------|----------------|-------|
| Change to program risk appetite (e.g., acceptance of higher false positive rate to catch more fraud) | Steering Committee | Requires written request 10 working days before meeting |
| Permanent removal of a seller category from the marketplace | Steering Committee | Interim suspensions permitted by Operational Working Group |
| New automated enforcement action type | Operational Working Group | Safety Engineering to present success criteria and rollback plan |
| Significant change to appeals process | Operational Working Group | With input from Policy |
| Cross-border data sharing arrangement | Steering Committee | Legal review required |
| Emergency account ban wave (>1,000 accounts) | Program Director, with immediate notification to Steering Committee Chair | Retrospective review at next Steering Committee |

### 7.2 Escalation Paths

Standard escalation for a single case follows: Analyst → Senior Analyst → Team Lead → Head of Operations → Program Director. Time-sensitive escalations (e.g., active scam campaign, payment fraud spike) go directly to the Head of Financial Crime or Head of Safety Engineering, bypassing the team lead layer.

For cases involving imminent physical harm, credible threats, or child safety material, the analyst contacts the dedicated safety liaison (via the 24/7 on-call roster) and the Regional Trust and Safety Lead immediately. These cases are flagged "CRITICAL – PERSONAL SAFETY" in the case management system and are exempt from standard SLA tracking.

## 8. Governance Cadence and Reporting

All meeting minutes are stored in the TrustAnchor SharePoint site under `Governance/YYYY/`. Action items are assigned in the minutes and tracked in the program risk register. KPI packs are published to the same site on the first working day of each month.

## 9. Program Scope

### 9.1 In Scope

The TrustAnchor program covers the following:

- Buyer and seller account integrity (unauthorised access, account takeover, impersonation)
- Listing integrity (counterfeit goods, prohibited items, misrepresentation)
- Transaction integrity (payment fraud, non-delivery, price manipulation)
- Post-transaction disputes (returns, refunds, chargebacks)
- User communication integrity (scam messages, phishing, off-platform solicitation)
- Platform abuse (fake reviews, vote manipulation, evasion of sanctions)

**Session 2024-03-11 (Mon) – Dispute Resolution Process Walkthrough**
Participants: JK, LM, NP, QR, ST, UV, WX, YZ, AB, CD, EF. 11 participants, mix of new and established sellers.

Session focused on walking through a sample dispute scenario: a buyer claims an item was not received, but tracking shows delivery. JK immediately said, "This is the part I hate. I did everything right and I still lose money." LM asked about the evidence submission deadline; clarified that it is 72 hours, but extensions are available under certain circumstances. NP queried whether courier GPS data is accepted as proof; yes, if it is from the integrated courier network. QR shared a past experience where a dispute was resolved in their favour after three weeks; QR noted, "I had to call twice to get an update, so I don't trust the timeline." ST asked about appeal rights after a decision; yes, one appeal within 14 days. UV raised a scenario about a buyer who claimed damage was caused by the courier; explained that the seller is not liable if the item was packaged per guidelines, but the seller must provide packaging photos. WX asked whether the dispute team has access to chat logs; yes, they do. YZ asked about partial refunds – whether they can be offered without a formal dispute; yes, this is encouraged for low-value items. AB asked about the fee structure for disputes; no fee for sellers. CD noted that the dispute form is confusing, specifically the "item condition" dropdown. EF asked whether a seller can withdraw from a dispute; yes, before the decision is made.

Facilitator note: the 72-hour evidence window is the most contentious point. Participants want more time, especially for international shipments. This was raised by at least six participants. Recommend reviewing this policy with the trust team. Also, CD's comment about the dropdown is a UX issue; submit as feedback.

**Session 2024-03-18 (Mon) – Trust Score Dashboard Introduction**
Participants: GH, IJ, KL, MN, OP, QR, ST, UV, WX, YZ. 10 participants, all with established accounts (>1 year).

This session introduced the trust score dashboard, which is currently in beta. GH asked how the score is calculated; explained that it is a composite of order completion, dispute rate, response time, and account age. IJ queried whether a single dispute significantly affects the score; answer: it depends on the outcome and the seller's overall volume. KL noted, "I check my dashboard every morning, so if the number drops I want to know why." This is a common sentiment; participants expect a breakdown or an explanation for any score change. MN asked whether the score is visible to buyers; not currently, but it may be in the future. OP asked about the refresh frequency; the score updates daily. QR, who had a dispute in February, asked whether the score would recover over time; yes, if no further issues. ST asked whether the score affects seller support priority; no, it does not. UV asked about the "at-risk" indicator; explained that it highlights sellers whose score dropped by more than 10 points in a week. WX asked whether the score is used for listing placement; not directly, but it may influence "recommended seller" badges in the future. YZ raised a privacy question: can sellers see the exact data used? Yes, via the "score details" tab.

Facilitator note: participants were more receptive to the dashboard than expected. The main concern is the lack of transparency around score changes. EF asked whether a listing removed for a policy violation counts against the seller's trust score; answer: it does not, unless the removal is part of a pattern. GH mentioned that they had a listing removed in error last year and the appeal took three weeks; asked if the SLA has improved. Explained the current target is five business days, but noted that during high-volume periods it can stretch. IJ asked whether sellers receive a notification when a report is filed against them; yes, but only after the review is complete, not at the time of the report. This was met with some surprise. KL said, "If someone reports me, I want to know about it right away so I can fix the problem before it escalates." OP asked whether repeat reporters are flagged; said we don't disclose that. documents.title: TrustAnchor Program Charter
documents.content:
### 3.1 Protect Marketplace Participants
- Reduce the incidence of fraudulent listings, counterfeit goods, and deceptive seller practices.
- Safeguard buyer payment information and personal data from unauthorised access.
- Provide clear reporting mechanisms and timely support for users who experience harm.

### 3.2 Maintain Platform Integrity
- Detect and remove coordinated inauthentic behaviour, including fake reviews, artificially inflated ratings, and seller collusion.
- Prevent the use of the marketplace for money laundering, sanctions evasion, or other illegal financial activity.
- Preserve the accuracy and reliability of product listings and transaction records.

### 3.3 Build User Confidence
- Increase transparency around trust and safety decisions, including appeal processes.
- Educate users on safe trading practices and common scam indicators.
- Publish regular trust and safety reports to demonstrate accountability.

### 3.4 Enable Responsible Growth
- Support legitimate sellers in scaling their operations without undue friction.
- Integrate trust and safety controls into new product features at the design stage.
- Balance enforcement with user experience to avoid unnecessary disruption.

## 4. Scope

TrustAnchor applies to all marketplace interactions involving:
- Consumer-to-consumer (C2C) sales
- Business-to-consumer (B2C) sales
- Auction listings
- Fixed-price listings
- Digital goods and services
- Payment processing and escrow services
- User-to-user messaging and communication features

The program does not cover logistics and shipping disputes unless they involve suspected fraud or safety risks. Employment, tax, and general legal compliance matters outside marketplace integrity are excluded.

## 5. Key Performance Indicators

The following KPIs are tracked monthly and reported quarterly to the Program Steering Committee. Baselines and targets are reviewed annually.

The TrustAnchor program charter records the program_launch_date as 2024-03-01. Record status: current.

| KPI ID | Metric | Baseline (2023) | Target (2024) | Target (2025) |
|--------|--------|-----------------|---------------|---------------|
| KPI-01 | Fraudulent listing removal rate (within 24h of report) | 61% | 75% | 85% |
| KPI-02 | Account takeover detection rate | 0.2% of active accounts | 0.35% | 0.5% |
| KPI-03 | Median time to resolve user safety reports | 96 hours | 72 hours | 48 hours |
| KPI-04 | Buyer satisfaction with dispute resolution | 3.1/5 | 3.6/5 | 4.0/5 |
| KPI-05 | Repeat offence rate among sanctioned sellers | 18% | 12% | 8% |
| KPI-06 | False positive rate on automated listing reviews | 6.5% | 4.0% | 3.0% |
| KPI-07 | User appeal success rate | 22% | 30% | 35% |
| KPI-08 | Proactive detection share of total enforcement | 41% | 55% | 65% |
| KPI-09 | Payment fraud loss rate | 1.1% of transaction value | 0.7% | 0.4% |
| KPI-10 | Time to remove confirmed scam accounts | 18 hours | 8 hours | 4 hours |

### 5.1 Measurement Notes
- KPI-01 excludes listings removed automatically by keyword filters.
- KPI-02 is measured against accounts with verified activity in the preceding 90 days.
- KPI-06 uses a sample of 10,000 reviewed listings per month.
- KPI-09 covers chargebacks and confirmed fraudulent transactions net of recoveries.

## 6. Governance Structure

The TrustAnchor program operates under a tiered governance model:

### 6.1 Program Steering Committee
- Chaired by the Chief Risk Officer
- Meets quarterly
- Reviews KPI performance, major incidents, and resource allocation
- Approves changes to program scope and risk appetite

## 7. Roles and Responsibilities

## 7. Roles and Responsibilities (continued)

| Role | Accountable For | Key Activities | Reporting Line |
|------|----------------|----------------|----------------|
| Program Director | Overall program delivery, KPI achievement, budget | Chairs Operational Working Group; owns program roadmap; approves policy interpretations; reports to Steering Committee | Chief Risk Officer |
| Head of Trust & Safety Policy | Policy framework, appeals framework, regulatory alignment | Drafts and maintains policy documents; leads appeals review; tracks legislative changes (ACCC, ACMA, OAIC) | Program Director |
| Head of Trust & Safety Operations | Day-to-day enforcement, queue management, SLA adherence | Manages analyst teams; owns investigation playbooks; monitors KPI-01, KPI-03, KPI-10 | Program Director |
| Head of Safety Engineering | Detection systems, automation, model performance | Owns KPI-02, KPI-06, KPI-08; prioritises feature development; manages vendor tooling | Program Director |
| Head of Financial Crime | Payment fraud, money laundering, sanctions screening | Owns KPI-09; coordinates with banking partners; manages chargeback dispute processes | Program Director |
| Regional Trust and Safety Lead – AU | Local implementation, AU regulatory engagement | Implements program in Australia; liaises with state/territory consumer affairs bodies; submits monthly reports | Program Director (dotted line to Regional GM) |
| Senior Trust and Safety Analyst (rotating) | Case quality, escalation triage | Reviews high-risk cases; identifies systemic issues; contributes to fortnightly Working Group | Head of Trust & Safety Operations |
| Data Analyst (dedicated) | KPI reporting, dashboard maintenance, ad hoc analysis | Produces monthly KPI pack; validates data quality; supports incident post-mortems | Head of Safety Engineering |

### 7.1 Decision Rights

The following decisions require escalation to the named forum. No single role may act unilaterally on these matters.

| Decision | Approving Forum | Notes |
|----------|----------------|-------|
| Change to program risk appetite (e.g., acceptance of higher false positive rate to catch more fraud) | Steering Committee | Requires written request 10 working days before meeting |
| Permanent removal of a seller category from the marketplace | Steering Committee | Interim suspensions permitted by Operational Working Group |
| New automated enforcement action type | Operational Working Group | Safety Engineering to present success criteria and rollback plan |
| Significant change to appeals process | Operational Working Group | With input from Policy |
| Cross-border data sharing arrangement | Steering Committee | Legal review required |
| Emergency account ban wave (>1,000 accounts) | Program Director, with immediate notification to Steering Committee Chair | Retrospective review at next Steering Committee |

### 7.2 Escalation Paths

Standard escalation for a single case follows: Analyst → Senior Analyst → Team Lead → Head of Operations → Program Director. Time-sensitive escalations (e.g., active scam campaign, payment fraud spike) go directly to the Head of Financial Crime or Head of Safety Engineering, bypassing the team lead layer.

For cases involving imminent physical harm, credible threats, or child safety material, the analyst contacts the dedicated safety liaison (via the 24/7 on-call roster) and the Regional Trust and Safety Lead immediately. These cases are flagged "CRITICAL – PERSONAL SAFETY" in the case management system and are exempt from standard SLA tracking.

## 8. Governance Cadence and Reporting

All meeting minutes are stored in the TrustAnchor SharePoint site under `Governance/YYYY/`. Action items are assigned in the minutes and tracked in the program risk register. KPI packs are published to the same site on the first working day of each month.

## 9. Program Scope

### 9.1 In Scope

The TrustAnchor program covers the following:

- Buyer and seller account integrity (unauthorised access, account takeover, impersonation)
- Listing integrity (counterfeit goods, prohibited items, misrepresentation)
- Transaction integrity (payment fraud, non-delivery, price manipulation)
- Post-transaction disputes (returns, refunds, chargebacks)
- User communication integrity (scam messages, phishing, off-platform solicitation)
- Platform abuse (fake reviews, vote manipulation, evasion of sanctions)

documents.title: Facilitator Session Notes
documents.content:
Key observation: the error messaging around document uploads is causing repeated attempts and frustration. Participants are not reading the help centre articles; they expect inline guidance. The session ran 10 minutes over because of the volume of questions on this topic. Note: follow up with AK regarding her specific upload error – screenshot taken.

---

**Session 2024-03-11 (Mon) – Dispute Resolution Process Walkthrough**
Participants: JK, LM, NP, QR, ST, UV, WX, YZ, AB, CD, EF. 11 participants, mix of new and established sellers.

Session focused on walking through a sample dispute scenario: a buyer claims an item was not received, but tracking shows delivery. JK immediately said, "This is the part I hate. I did everything right and I still lose money." LM asked about the evidence submission deadline; clarified that it is 72 hours, but extensions are available under certain circumstances. NP queried whether courier GPS data is accepted as proof; yes, if it is from the integrated courier network. QR shared a past experience where a dispute was resolved in their favour after three weeks; QR noted, "I had to call twice to get an update, so I don't trust the timeline." ST asked about appeal rights after a decision; yes, one appeal within 14 days. UV raised a scenario about a buyer who claimed damage was caused by the courier; explained that the seller is not liable if the item was packaged per guidelines, but the seller must provide packaging photos. WX asked whether the dispute team has access to chat logs; yes, they do. YZ asked about partial refunds – whether they can be offered without a formal dispute; yes, this is encouraged for low-value items. AB asked about the fee structure for disputes; no fee for sellers. CD noted that the dispute form is confusing, specifically the "item condition" dropdown. EF asked whether a seller can withdraw from a dispute; yes, before the decision is made.

Facilitator note: the 72-hour evidence window is the most contentious point. Participants want more time, especially for international shipments. This was raised by at least six participants. Recommend reviewing this policy with the trust team. Also, CD's comment about the dropdown is a UX issue; submit as feedback.

---

The Facilitator Notes System note_count is 356 notes. Record status: current.

**Session 2024-03-18 (Mon) – Trust Score Dashboard Introduction**
Participants: GH, IJ, KL, MN, OP, QR, ST, UV, WX, YZ. 10 participants, all with established accounts (>1 year).

This session introduced the trust score dashboard, which is currently in beta. GH asked how the score is calculated; explained that it is a composite of order completion, dispute rate, response time, and account age. IJ queried whether a single dispute significantly affects the score; answer: it depends on the outcome and the seller's overall volume. KL noted, "I check my dashboard every morning, so if the number drops I want to know why." This is a common sentiment; participants expect a breakdown or an explanation for any score change. MN asked whether the score is visible to buyers; not currently, but it may be in the future. OP asked about the refresh frequency; the score updates daily. QR, who had a dispute in February, asked whether the score would recover over time; yes, if no further issues. ST asked whether the score affects seller support priority; no, it does not. UV asked about the "at-risk" indicator; explained that it highlights sellers whose score dropped by more than 10 points in a week. WX asked whether the score is used for listing placement; not directly, but it may influence "recommended seller" badges in the future. YZ raised a privacy question: can sellers see the exact data used? Yes, via the "score details" tab.

Facilitator note: participants were more receptive to the dashboard than expected. The main concern is the lack of transparency around score changes. Several participants mentioned they would like email alerts when the score changes significantly. This is a potential feature request. Also, the "at-risk" indicator caused some anxiety; clarify the threshold in the documentation.

documents.title: Facilitator Session Notes
documents.content:
**Session 2024-04-15 (Mon) – Trust & Safety Reporting Workflow**

Participants: AB, CD, EF, GH, IJ, KL, MN, OP, QR, ST. 10 participants, mixed seller types.

Follow-up to the listing policy session. AB asked whether the new prohibited-items list applies to existing listings or only new ones; answer: existing listings must be removed within 14 days of the notice. CD raised a concern about the appeals process — said the form is hard to find. Walked through the location on the seller dashboard. Several participants nodded; this might be a discoverability issue worth flagging to the product team. EF asked whether a listing removed for a policy violation counts against the seller's trust score; answer: it does not, unless the removal is part of a pattern. GH mentioned that they had a listing removed in error last year and the appeal took three weeks; asked if the SLA has improved. Explained the current target is five business days, but noted that during high-volume periods it can stretch. IJ asked whether sellers receive a notification when a report is filed against them; yes, but only after the review is complete, not at the time of the report. This was met with some surprise. KL said, "If someone reports me, I want to know about it right away so I can fix the problem before it escalates." OP asked whether repeat reporters are flagged; said we don't disclose that. QR asked about the difference between a report and a dispute; clarified: a report is about a listing or behaviour, a dispute is about a transaction. ST asked whether the reporting workflow is available on mobile; yes, but the appeals form is desktop-only at this stage.

Facilitator note: the group was most engaged when discussing notification timing. There is a clear expectation gap — sellers assume they will be told about reports immediately. Worth capturing as a feature request. Also, the appeals form discoverability issue came up independently of my prompt, which suggests it is a real pain point.

---

**Session 2024-04-29 (Mon) – Payment Hold Policy**

Participants: GH, IJ, KL, MN, OP, QR, ST, UV, WX, YZ. 10 participants, all with established accounts (>1 year).

This session covered the payment hold policy for new sellers and for sellers with recent disputes. GH asked why holds are applied to established accounts; explained that a hold can be triggered by a spike in dispute rate or a chargeback. IJ asked how long a hold lasts; standard is 7 days after delivery confirmation, but it can extend to 21 days if there is an open dispute. KL asked whether interest is paid on held funds; no. MN noted that they had a hold in January and the communication was unclear — said, "I only found out about the hold when a buyer asked where their refund was." OP asked whether sellers can request an early release; yes, if the buyer confirms receipt. QR asked whether the hold policy is disclosed at registration; it is in the terms of service, but the group generally agreed that this is not prominent enough. ST asked whether holds affect the trust score; no, they are separate. UV asked about the appeals process for holds; directed to the same form as listing appeals, which prompted a few eye rolls. WX asked whether there is a cap on the number of holds per month; no, but each hold is reviewed individually. YZ asked whether the hold amount is based on the transaction value or the account balance; transaction value.

Facilitator note: the group was frustrated about communication during holds. The January hold example from MN was detailed — they received a generic email with no reference number, and the support chat took four days to respond. This is consistent with feedback from other sessions. Also, the terms of service point came up again; sellers want a plain-language summary at the point of registration. I will include this in the summary.
